It stays at the floor (0.00-0.25 of the 2.15 max) on the very same token ' of' when the preceding noun is self-sufficient ('the table/title/cover/index/center/corner/size/color of X') and on the trailing piece of a common word the model already resolved from its first piece ('microbi|ology', 'dermat|ology', 'gast|ric', 'Chel|ten|ham', 'Ave|bury'), so what predicts it is whether the current token is bound into a larger unit rather than which token it is.

The museum's new exhibition on ancient Mesopotamia opened on a grey Thursday morning, and by noon the queue stretched past the gift shop and out onto the pavement. Curators had spent three years assembling the collection, borrowing clay tablets from institutions in Berlin, Baghdad and Philadelphia, and the result is a dense, sometimes overwhelming show that rewards slow walking. Visitors enter through a narrow corridor lined with photographs of the excavation sites, then pass into a hall dominated by a reconstructed gate. A wall label credits the original structure to Nebuchadnezzar II and notes that only the foundations survive.

From there the exhibition turns to daily life. Cases of cuneiform tablets record barley deliveries, complaints about late payments and a surprisingly tender letter from a father to his son. A short film, projected onto a curved screen, follows a team of archaeologists through a season of digging. The soundtrack is mostly wind and the scrape of trowels, and several visitors in the gallery that morning stayed through two full screenings.

Earlier in the week, a school group from Leeds had been the first to see the finished installation. Their teacher said the children had expected dusty cases of broken pots and were instead captivated by the flickering lamps and the low, looping music. Several asked whether the hall could be booked for a school dinner, a question the curators are still considering.

The final rooms are quieter. Pottery shards are arranged in long rows, each with a typed card explaining where it was found and what it once held. School groups drift through in noisy bursts, then leave the space silent again. Near the exit, a case of cylinder seals invites visitors to press a button and watch an illuminated replica roll out an impression in wax.

The exhibition's centrepiece, though, sits in the middle of the last gallery: a life-size reconstruction of a banqueting hall, lit by low lamps that flicker at irregular intervals. Reeds, baskets and low tables are arranged as they might have been four thousand years ago, and a faint recording of a lyre plays on a loop. Visitors tend to fall silent here, walking slowly around the installation and reading the labels in whispers.

Outside, the afternoon had brightened and the queue had shortened to a dozen people. The gift shop sold out of the exhibition catalogue before three o'clock. Curators say the show will travel to two other cities next year, though the reconstruction will stay behind, too fragile to move. For anyone who has walked the galleries, the image that lingers is not the gold or the tablets but that dim hall, its lamps still flickering, its tables set for guests who never arrive.
